This study also considered the effects of various probe options particularly to ensure damage to cells were minimized. At the time of this study the probe utilized was a LSP S4 capable of 0.02N-0.16N of contact trigger force required depending on the required measurement settings. Unfortunately this low force probe still imparted marks on the order of 50-80nm on soft copper surfaces. Leitz was also developing an even lower force capable LSP S4 ANF version to decrease this probing force down to 0.005N, although this product seems to have not yet made it market. For in-process inspection of less precise features, such as during conventional braze stack up or just prior to RF cold test measurements, a laser tracker may be the best option and can be used to validate full assembly form. Laser trackers are also the device of choice for final AS fiducialization where precision geometries of the AS are related to fiducial cup locations to be utilized during the beamline installation survey group alignment process. B.1.4 Precision of machining/cost versus requirements for manual tuning of structure Often one of the highest individual labor costs associated with any AS is with final RF cold testing and tuning. For critical AS this is almost always performed by experienced PhD scientists and requires an in-depth understanding of RF performance sensitives and their relationships to device performance. Although it is not possible to entirely eliminate the critical task of final device RF characterization, the effort required to tune a structure can potentially be reduced or eliminated through higher precision manufacturing. The cost implications of such a decision requires a more in-depth analysis than can be provided in this report, however Page 12 of 55 “Manufacturing full-scale high gradient copper accelerators: Electron beam welding and allied processes” Prepared for the U.S. Department of Energy ARDAP program an initial qualitative assessment concludes that the 2um level precision and accuracy required to achieve this goal may not bring significant value and may also incur risks associated with final device rejection due to the omission of tuning provisions. The piece part rejection rate; utilization of the world’s highest class of machine tools and CMM equipment; the longer cutting cycles; along with the caliber of staff required to operate these machines do not seem to justify the RF scientist labor reduction. There would be no saving in tooling either, as the same equipment such as vector network analyzers and measurement stands would have to be developed regardless in order to perform cold test qualification. It is prudent to note however that by determining a reasonable tolerance band to target as a function of manufacturing cost and tuning costs would be prudent in order to ensure that part and AS yields are high. Further depending on the device construction, deformation based tuning may also introduce modes within a structure, which when excessive, could affect the device performance quality.
